blocks.text: Read the chapter with this setting in view: Isaiah 25-27 and 65-66 use death-defeat, bodily revival, transformed longevity, renewed Jerusalem, and new-heavens-and-earth imagery that becomes foundational for later Jewish and Christian resurrection and new-creation hope. It gives a starting point for following the chapter's own movement. The chapter itself should determine how far the point is taken. Interpretations differ on some details.

For its historical and cultural setting, note that Paul combines death-swallowed and death-taunt scriptural language with thanksgiving and a call to steadfast labor because such labor is not empty. This background clarifies the setting assumed by the passage. It does not by itself settle every question raised by the chapter. The evidence leaves some details unresolved.

A literary feature to notice is that The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete sixty-six-chapter witness broadly aligned with the Masoretic tradition but containing thousands of orthographic and substantive differences; other Qumran Isaiah manuscripts and pesharim show active transmission and interpretation. This form helps organize the chapter's claims. Notice it before drawing broader conclusions from a single phrase or image. The evidence leaves some details unresolved.
